title: Franz Kafka, The Metamorphosis recast
author: tbr
note: A breadwinner wakes wrong; the family ledger of duty and relief does the rest. After Kafka, The Metamorphosis, 1915.

scenes.title: The apartment
scenes.reentry: Gregor Samsa woke from uneasy dreams and found himself changed into something that would not fit under the covers.

breaths.text: Gregor Samsa woke from uneasy dreams and found himself changed into something that would not fit under the covers.
He did not have a name for it.
His back was hard.
His legs—too many—moved when he did not ask them to.
The ceiling looked the same.
The alarm on the nightstand kept its red digits.
Outside, a bus sighed at the corner stop.
He tried to turn onto his side and heard a dry scrape against the sheet.
Panic rose, then a practical thought, almost automatic: he would be late for the warehouse route.
His phone buzzed once against the wood—dispatch—and fell still.
He reached with what had been an arm and knocked the phone to the floor, where it lit the dust underneath the bed like a small, trapped moon.
His mother knocked.
"Gregor?
You're not up."
His father's heavier tread followed in the hall.
Grete, his sister, called that coffee was ready.
Their voices were ordinary.
The ordinary made the room tilt.
He answered, or tried to.
What came out was a rasp that startled even him.
Silence on the other side of the door.
Then his father: "Open up.
The supervisor already texted."
Keys scratched.
The lock turned.
The door opened a hand's width and stopped.
Grete saw him first.
She did not scream.
She made a small sound, as if she had bitten her tongue, and shoved the door shut.
From the hall came whispering, rapid and ugly.
Gregor lay very still, listening to his family rearrange themselves around the fact of him.
In the days that followed, the apartment learned a new choreography.
Food was left just inside the door—milk going warm, then scraps, then nothing anyone would admit to preparing.
Grete was the bravest.
She entered with a broom held like a weapon and her face turned sideways, and she cleaned around him with a fierce, tearful competence.
His mother prayed in the kitchen.
His father stopped looking at the closed door and started looking at bills on the table, as if numbers could replace a son.
Gregor understood, in the slow way of someone who has always paid for everyone, that he was no longer useful.
The route went to someone else.
The insurance calls began.
His father's voice through the wall grew louder at strangers and quieter at home.

Once, when Gregor dragged himself toward the living room at night, desperate for the window's cool air, his father drove him back with a rolled magazine and a shoe, breathing hard, eyes wet with something that was not only rage.
Grete brought a violin case home from her lessons and practiced with the door open, as if music might make the apartment a place again.
Gregor crept closer, drawn by the thin line of melody.
She saw him and stopped mid-phrase.
The bow hung in the air.
Her face closed.
"It has to go," she said to their parents, not looking at Gregor.
"If it were Gregor, it would have left us already.
This thing only makes us sick."
His mother wept.
His father nodded once, relieved to be given permission.
Gregor retreated to the room that had been his and felt, with a clarity that hurt less than expecting love, that he was already practicing absence.
He stopped eating.
The apple his father had thrown days earlier still sat, browned and soft, against his side where the skin had broken.
Dust settled on his back.
Through the thin wall he heard Grete laugh at a video on her phone—brief, young, alive—and the sound did not include him.
One morning the cleaner found him dry and still near the baseboard.
Grete covered him with a sheet without touching what was under it.
His father put a hand on her shoulder.
His mother opened a window.
The apartment smelled, briefly, of cold air and relief.
That evening they took the bus to the edge of the city and walked where the light was longer.
Grete stretched her arms and the wind moved her hair.
Her parents watched her as if she were a future they could afford again.
Behind them, in a room that would be cleared by the weekend, the last of Gregor's usefulness finished becoming someone else's problem.
